content: 1. In areas where there has been no program of regular preventive chemotherapy, a clinical approach of test-and-treat should be considered instead of population-wide preventive chemotherapy. This recommendation is conditional, with very low certainty of evidence. 2. Close epidemiological monitoring should be established to track the prevalence of Schistosoma species, particularly in settings where the prevalence was previously ≥10% or where preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel has been reduced in frequency. Monitoring should include sentinel site surveys or mid-term evaluations every three years. 3. In endemic communities with a prevalence of Schistosoma infections ≥10% that show inadequate response to annual preventive chemotherapy (despite achieving ≥75% treatment coverage), the WHO suggests considering biannual (twice-yearly) preventive chemotherapy instead of annual treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 4. An inadequate response is defined as less than a one-third relative reduction in prevalence when comparing baseline prevalence surveys with repeat surveys conducted after two years of annual preventive chemotherapy. The intervening period should include at least two rounds of preventive chemotherapy with adequate treatment coverage (≥75%) for all at-risk groups. 5. Alternative definitions of inadequate response could consider absolute changes in infection prevalence or changes in the average intensity of infection (e.g., egg concentrations in stool or urine). 6. Prevalence surveys should account for the seasonality of transmission to ensure that measurements are taken at the same point in each seasonal transmission cycle. 7. Communities suspected to be persistent hotspots or of high endemicity (baseline prevalence ≥50% in school-aged children) are encouraged to conduct early prevalence surveys (after two annual rounds of preventive chemotherapy) to inform decisions on biannual treatment. 8. Biannual preventive chemotherapy should be prioritized in areas of higher prevalence (baseline prevalence ≥50% in school-aged children and persistent hotspot settings) that have already achieved high levels of annual treatment coverage without an appropriate response. In moderate-prevalence settings (10–49% prevalence in school-aged children), annual treatment may suffice. 9. Routine monitoring of treatment coverage should be an integral part of preventive chemotherapy programs, ensuring that annual treatment achieves high coverage (≥75%) before transitioning to biannual treatment. 10. There is currently insufficient evidence to determine the optimal duration of biannual treatment. As an interim measure, three consecutive years of biannual preventive chemotherapy are suggested, followed by an impact survey to assess whether the frequency should be continued or reduced. 11. Biannual treatment programs will require a larger global supply of praziquantel than is currently available through donation schemes (estimated at 300 million tablets annually at the time of publication). 12. Biannual treatment administrations should be spaced approximately six months apart throughout the year. 13. WHO recommends that health facilities provide access to praziquantel treatment to control morbidity due to schistosomiasis in all infected individuals, regardless of age, including infected pregnant women (excluding the first trimester), lactating women, and children under two years of age. Treatment decisions for children under two should be based on testing and clinical judgment. 14. Pregnancy status should be assessed discreetly by questioning the individual. If uncertain, a negative urine-based pregnancy test can be requested before administering treatment. 15. For children under two years of age, the medicine should ideally be in an oral formulation (currently under development) that is easy to administer, disintegrates in the mouth, and has a sweet taste and smell. If pediatric formulations are unavailable, crushed praziquantel in soft food may be used for individual case treatment only. 16. WHO strongly recommends WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) interventions, environmental interventions (e.g., water engineering and focal snail control with molluscicides), and behavioral change interventions as essential measures to reduce Schistosoma transmission in endemic areas. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 17. WASH interventions are expected to provide modest benefits in limiting Schistosoma transmission, with additional benefits in reducing the risk of multiple infectious diseases. 18. Behavioral change interventions should be implemented from the start of any preventive chemotherapy program. 19. Coordination and joint planning between schistosomiasis control programs and WASH initiatives are essential. This includes mapping and sharing epidemiological information alongside WASH coverage to prioritize water and sanitation services in endemic areas. 20. Schistosomiasis education and health program delivery should include inputs to WASH program design, collaboration on behavioral change interventions, and integration of behavioral change promotion. 21. In areas where persistent hotspots of transmission emerge during preventive chemotherapy campaigns, controlling intermediate host snail populations should be prioritized, especially if the program is already achieving high levels of treatment coverage. 22. Co-implementation of snail control with mass treatment campaigns is expected to accelerate the achievement of WHO goals for morbidity control and elimination as a public health problem. 23. Snail control will be essential to ultimately eliminate local transmission, in combination with WASH interventions. 24. Public health awareness campaigns will be necessary to ensure high acceptance of snail control interventions. 25. Developing snail control programs will require a larger and less expensive global supply of molluscicides. 26. Skilled and dedicated snail control workers will be essential for the success of snail control initiatives. 27. Deworming should be delivered alongside health and hygiene promotion to reduce transmission by encouraging healthy behaviors, such as proper disposal of feces. 28. Testing for Schistosoma infection in humans should use diagnostics with high sensitivity and specificity. This may require a two-step diagnostic process, starting with a highly sensitive test followed by a confirmatory test with high specificity. 29. Testing for Schistosoma infection in snails should also use diagnostics with high sensitivity and specificity, potentially requiring a two-step diagnostic process. 30. Testing for Schistosoma infection in non-human mammalian hosts, where applicable, should follow similar diagnostic standards, with a two-step process if necessary. 31. The predictive performance of sampling humans, snails, and non-human mammalian hosts to identify settings that have eliminated transmission will depend on the sampling strategy, including decisions on sample size, geographical zones, and timespan for sampling. 32. Future work could consider a two-step verification of Schistosoma infection status in humans, using a highly sensitive test (e.g., serology) followed by a confirmatory highly specific test (e.g., miracidia hatching test). 33. Sampling and diagnostic tools in snail populations and non-human mammalian hosts should be considered when the public health goal is to interrupt transmission, as suggested by recent epidemiological surveys in human populations. 34. The contribution of non-human mammalian hosts to Schistosoma transmission remains under-studied, particularly for species other than S. japonicum. 35. Human schistosomiasis is an acute and chronic parasitic disease caused by infection with blood flukes (Schistosoma species). It is transmitted when humans or infected animal hosts contaminate freshwater sources with excreta containing parasite eggs, which hatch in water. People become infected when larval forms of the parasite penetrate the skin during contact with infested water. 36. Adult worms live in blood vessels, where females release eggs after mating with males. Some eggs are excreted in feces or urine to continue the parasite's life cycle, while others become trapped in body tissues, causing immune reactions that progressively damage organs. 37. Preventive chemotherapy, defined as large-scale preventive treatment with safe, single-dose, quality-assured medicines, is the core public health strategy for controlling and eliminating schistosomiasis.
